If there are gods, but unjust, then you should not want to worship them. If there are no gods, then you will be gone, but will have lived a noble life that will live on in the memories of your loved ones

answer.label: Not Marcus Aurelius — a modern fabrication
answer.authorDates: Circulating online since the mid-2000s; not from antiquity
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording appears nowhere in Marcus Aurelius’s ‘Meditations’ or any other ancient source, and no printed citation predates the internet. It is a modern, anonymous composition that loosely echoes — and actually reverses — a genuine passage, ‘Meditations’ 2.11, where Marcus insists the gods do exist and do care for humankind. The agnostic, ‘if there are no gods’ framing is foreign to him.

source.heading: What Marcus Aurelius actually wrote

docMeta.dd: Not in this or any ancient text — modern fabrication

source.excerpt: Since it is possible that thou mayest depart from life this very moment, regulate every act and thought accordingly. But to go away from among men, if there are gods, is not a thing to be afraid of, for the gods will not involve thee in evil; but if indeed they do not exist, or if they have no concern about human affairs, why should I desire to live in a universe devoid of gods and devoid of Providence? But in truth they do exist, and they do care for human things.
trail: The quote “appears nowhere in his single extant work… there is no indication that Marcus Aurelius ever said anything of the sort,” per the source-checking analysis at Three Shouts on a Hilltop.
The line is “fabricated based loosely on” the authentic ‘Meditations’ 2.11, whose meaning it reverses — Undeniably Atheist.
The genuine 2.11 text — “if gods exist… they would not involve you in ill… But they do exist, and they do care for men’s lives” — can be read at Wikisource.
Discussion tracing the wording to the internet rather than any print source: Hacker News thread.
source.excerptNote: The genuine passage (George Long’s 1862 translation). Note how it affirms the gods and their care — the opposite of the ‘if there are gods, but unjust… if there are no gods’ construction in the viral quote.

sourceLink.text: Meditations, Book 2 (George Long translation) at the Internet Classics Archive

source.rightsNote: The viral wording is an anonymous modern composition with no identifiable author or first-publication record, so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted for it. The genuine ‘Meditations’ is ancient and long in the public domain; the specific 1862 George Long translation quoted above is itself public domain, while some modern translations (e.g. Farquharson 1944, Hays 2002) remain in copyright.

author.name: Marcus Aurelius
author.heading: The emperor who never wrote it
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus ruled Rome from 161 to 180 AD and is remembered as the last of the ‘Five Good Emperors.’ His private notebook, the ‘Meditations,’ is a cornerstone of Stoic philosophy — and a devout one: he repeatedly affirms the gods and their providence. That devotion is precisely why the agnostic ‘if there are no gods’ quote pinned to his name rings false.

misattribution.heading: Why it isn't Marcus Aurelius
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s classic ‘Stoic emperor’ fabrications: an eloquent, agnostic-friendly credo pinned on Marcus Aurelius’s name to borrow his authority.

items.why: The wording is absent from the ‘Meditations’ (his only work) and every other ancient source; the earliest traces are internet posts, with no printed citation found before roughly 2009, per Three Shouts on a Hilltop.

It is loosely modelled on the real ‘Meditations’ 2.11 but inverts its point: Marcus argues the gods do exist and care for us, whereas the fake floats the possibility of no gods, or unjust ones — a framing alien to a devout polytheist.

misattribution.truthLine: What Marcus really wrote is the calmer, God-affirming reflection of ‘Meditations’ 2.11 — not the ‘if there are no gods’ wager that now circulates under his name (Wikisource, Book 2).

context.heading: A modern wager in ancient dress
lead: The sentiment — live well and you lose nothing whether or not the gods are watching — is really a compact, secular restatement of Pascal’s Wager, dressed in Stoic robes. Its appeal is exactly why it spread: it flatters both the devout and the doubtful, and Marcus Aurelius’s reputation as the philosopher-king lends it instant gravitas.

But Marcus was an earnest polytheist for whom providence was a settled fact, not a hypothesis. The genuine passage it borrows from reaches the opposite conclusion: he would not even want to live ‘in a universe devoid of gods and devoid of Providence.’
context.pull: Marcus argues the gods do exist and care for us. The viral quote hedges that they might not exist at all.
